passages.t: Into Egypt, taking Jeremiah with them
passages.happening:
When Jeremiah finishes telling the people everything the LORD had sent him to say (verse 1), Azariah son of Hoshaiah, Johanan son of Kareah and all the arrogant men tell him he is lying. They say the LORD has not sent him to forbid them to go to Egypt (verse 2). Baruch son of Neriah, they say, is turning him against them, to hand them over to the Chaldeans to be killed or exiled (verse 3).

So Johanan and the commanders do not obey the LORD's command to stay in Judah (verse 4). They take the whole remnant, those who had come back from the nations where they were scattered (verse 5): men, women and children, the king's daughters, everyone Nebuzaradan had left with Gedaliah, and Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch son of Neriah (verse 6). ‘So they entered the land of Egypt because they did not obey the voice of the LORD, and they went as far as Tahpanhes’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The people had sworn to obey whatever God said. When the answer came, they called the prophet a liar and blamed his scribe. It was easier to accuse Baruch than to admit they did not want God's word.

They took Jeremiah with them. He had chosen to stay among the poor in Judah, and now he was carried off to Egypt against his will. Nothing is told of his later life beyond these chapters.

Tahpanhes was a frontier town on the eastern edge of the Nile Delta, known to Greek writers as Daphnae and identified with Tell Defenneh. It lay on the main road from Canaan into Egypt and held a garrison that included foreign soldiers, Greeks among them, serving the pharaohs.
passages.later: Isaiah had warned long before against those who ‘go down to Egypt for help’ (Isaiah 31:1). Kings tells the same flight: ‘all the people small and great’ fled to Egypt (2 Kings 25:26).
passages.asks: The people called God's word a lie when it did not suit them. Ask whether you have ever blamed the messenger for a message you did not want. And ask what it means that Jeremiah went on speaking even when carried where he did not want to go.

passages.happening:
At Tahpanhes the word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah (verse 8). In the sight of the Judeans he is to take large stones and bury them in the clay of the brick pavement at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace (verse 9).

Then he is to tell them that God will send for his servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and set his throne over these stones, and he will spread his royal canopy over them (verse 10). He will strike the land of Egypt, bringing death to those meant for death, captivity to those meant for captivity, and the sword to those meant for the sword (verse 11). God will kindle a fire in the temples of Egypt's gods; Nebuchadnezzar will burn them and carry off their gods, and wrap himself in Egypt as a shepherd wraps himself in his cloak (verse 12). He will break the sacred pillars of the temple of the sun and burn the temples of Egypt's gods (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Jeremiah's last sign-act is done in Egypt. The stones mark the spot where Babylon's king will one day set his throne. The people ran to Egypt to escape Babylon, and Babylon would follow them there.

When Flinders Petrie dug at Tell Defenneh in 1886, he found a large fortified building with a brick platform in front of it and suggested it was the place of verse 9. The identification is uncertain.

The temple of the sun was at Heliopolis, called On in the Bible, a great center of Egyptian worship famous for its stone obelisks, the sacred pillars of verse 13.
passages.later: Ezekiel also says God gave Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar: ‘I will give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon’ (Ezekiel 29:19). Joseph's wife Asenath was the daughter of a priest of On, the city of the sun (Genesis 41:45).
passages.hard:
Did Nebuchadnezzar actually conquer Egypt as Jeremiah said?

The historical record is limited. A fragmentary Babylonian tablet mentions a campaign against Egypt around 568 or 567 BC, and Ezekiel 29:17-20 also speaks of God giving Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar. But there is no evidence that Babylon occupied Egypt or destroyed Heliopolis in the way these verses picture, and Egypt stayed independent until the Persians conquered it in 525 BC. Some interpreters think the invasion of about 568 BC did real damage and fulfilled the prophecy in substance, even if the surviving records say little. Others read the vivid language, burning temples and Egypt wrapped like a cloak, as the stock imagery of conquest, fulfilled in Babylon's power over Egypt rather than in every detail.

These notes give both readings and do not choose between them.
passages.asks: The people ran to Egypt to escape Babylon, and God said Babylon would follow them there. Ask what you have run to that cannot actually protect you. And ask what it would take to stop running and trust God where you are.
